periods.name: Neolithic
details: The guide dates this as the longest listed span, roughly 10,000–3,000 BCE.
It ends around Uruk; agriculture, domestication, and towns developed across this long span.
periods.significance: Frames the long transition toward more settled agricultural communities.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Uruk Period (Mesopotamia)
details: The period saw some of the earliest cities and state formation in Mesopotamia.
Proto-writing and accounting practices developed alongside large-scale provisioning.
periods.significance: A key period for early urban organization and record keeping.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Old Kingdom, Egypt
details: Egyptian pyramid age, including Khufu’s Great Pyramid at Giza.
Monumental construction reflects the state’s capacity to organize labor.
periods.significance: Shows the scale of royal monuments and state organization.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Old Babylonian Period (Mesopotamia)
details: Hammurabi ruled in this period and commissioned his famous stele.
The stele is royal propaganda; earlier law collections existed.
periods.significance: Places Hammurabi’s royal justice claims in their historical context.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: New Kingdom, Egypt
details: Akhenaten founded Amarna as a new capital focused on the Aten.
The royal family’s Aten imagery reflects religious and artistic change.
periods.significance: Connects imperial Egypt with Amarna’s royal and religious changes.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Early and Middle Napatan Period, Sudan
details: The guide describes a strong Kushite kingdom at Napata.
Napatan rulers eventually challenged Assyrians for control of the southern Levant.
periods.significance: Shows Kush as a regional power interacting with Egypt and Assyria.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Neo-Assyrian Period
details: Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III are key rulers on the user’s card list.
Palace reliefs, the banquet stele, and the Black Obelisk display kingship and tribute.
periods.significance: A period of imperial expansion and representation of subject peoples.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Achaemenid Period
details: Cyrus and Darius I are major rulers in the user’s card list.
The Cyrus Cylinder and Persepolis reliefs represent royal legitimacy and imperial diversity.
periods.significance: Shows how Achaemenid kings represented political legitimacy and imperial diversity.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Hellenistic Kingdoms (Seleucid)
details: These kingdoms followed Alexander’s conquest; the Seleucids were one of them.
The guide permits “Seleucid” and “Hellenistic Kingdoms” interchangeably on the test.
periods.significance: Helps trace political succession and cultural exchange after Alexander.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Roman and Byzantine kingdoms
details: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians addresses an early Christian community.
Christianity later became a state-backed religious movement under Roman rule.
periods.significance: Provides the political context for Christianity’s growth through Late Antiquity.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Sasanian Period
details: Ardashir established Sasanian rule and appeared in investiture imagery.
The empire patronized Zoroastrian institutions while Mesopotamian magic bowls reveal mixed everyday practice.
periods.significance: Connects state religious policy to religious diversity on the ground.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

periods.name: Late Antiquity
details: The guide describes social and political reconfiguration as ancient writing systems fell out of use.
Christianity, Islam, and Zoroastrianism, and to some degree Judaism, rose as state-backed movements.
periods.significance: Frames the transformation of political and religious life from the early CE centuries to 850 CE.
periods.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Uruk vase
details: Alabaster vessel arranged in stacked registers: water and crops, sheep, then nude men carrying produce.
The upper register shows offerings to Inanna with a ruler at the front.
items.significance: Expresses ordered hierarchy and surplus flowing to the temple, an early state institution.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Beveled-rim bowls
details: Crude, mass-produced vessels made to a standard size; found by the hundreds of thousands.
Likely ration bowls used to distribute food to workers.
items.significance: Evidence for administered labor and bureaucracy during state formation.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Bulla and tokens
items.date: Tokens from Neolithic onward; bullae c. 3500–3100 BCE
details: Clay tokens represented goods and were sealed inside clay envelopes (bullae).
Tokens were pressed onto the outside of envelopes, leaving impressions.
items.significance: Shows that writing grew from accounting and administration, not literature.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Çatalhöyük
details: Dense mudbrick settlement with no streets and access to homes from rooftops.
Burials under floors, wall paintings, and bull horns are among its notable features.
items.significance: A large sedentary settlement without clear evidence of a state or elite.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Hammurabi's stele
details: Basalt monument depicting Hammurabi before Shamash and bearing about 282 laws.
The laws prescribe different outcomes according to social class.
items.significance: Not the first law code (Ur-Namma is earlier); it presents royal propaganda of the just king.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Khufu's Great Pyramid
details: About 146 m high and built from roughly 2.3 million blocks.
Nearby workers’ villages show organized, fed labor crews.
items.significance: Shows state power to organize labor; the claim that enslaved people built the pyramid is a myth.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Amarna
details: Akhenaten founded the city as a new capital dedicated to the Aten.
The city was abandoned after Akhenaten; the Amarna Letters are written in Akkadian cuneiform.
items.significance: Shows religious upheaval and international diplomacy in the New Kingdom.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Plaque of Akhenaten and Nefertiti under the Aten
details: The royal family appears beneath the sun disk, whose rays end in hands holding ankhs.
The figures use the elongated style associated with Amarna art.
items.significance: Presents Atenism, with the royal family as the channel to the god, and a break with tradition.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Kush/Nubia
items.date: Kerma c. 2500–1500 BCE; Napata c. 1100–650 BCE
items.location: Nile Valley in Sudan and southern Egypt
details: Kush was a rival of Egypt; Kushite kings ruled Egypt as its 25th Dynasty.
Kushite rulers also fought Assyria; the kingdom’s centers included Kerma and Napata.
items.significance: Centers African political history as an Egyptian peer and challenges Egypt-centered and racialized narratives.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Kerma elite tomb
details: Round graves have a circular stone pile at the entry.
Cattle skulls and food or drink offerings were placed outside the tombs.
items.significance: Shows distinct Kerma burial practices during a period of Kushite power.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Ashurnasirpal II's Banquet Stele
details: Celebrates the new capital and a ten-day feast for 69,574 guests.
The inscription lists food and building works.
items.significance: Projects royal abundance and empire through a gathering of guests from many communities.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Throneroom and courtyard reliefs of Ashurnasirpal II
details: Religious scenes show the king with winged spirits beside a sacred tree.
Tribute scenes show foreigners bringing goods; lamassu guard palace entrances.
items.significance: Depicts divinely backed kingship and tribute from conquered peoples.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Shalmaneser III's Black Obelisk
details: Black limestone monument with five registers of tribute.
One register shows Jehu of Israel bowing before the Assyrian king.
items.significance: Shows Assyrian domination of the Levant and links to people named in the Hebrew Bible.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Cyrus Cylinder
details: Akkadian cuneiform text says Marduk chose Cyrus over Nabonidus.
It describes temple restoration and the return of deported peoples.
items.significance: Not a first human-rights charter: it uses standard Mesopotamian royal propaganda. Pair with Isaiah 44–45.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Persepolis Reliefs
items.date: Begun ~518 BCE under Darius I; Achaemenid period
details: Apadana stairways show about 23 subject peoples bringing gifts in distinct dress.
Alexander burned Persepolis in 330 BCE.
items.significance: Depicts an ideology of harmonious multiethnic empire and how imperial difference was represented.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Isaiah 44–45
items.date: ~540s BCE; end of the Babylonian exile
details: Second Isaiah calls Cyrus God’s “anointed” and “shepherd,” who will rebuild Jerusalem.
The passage mocks idols and asserts one god.
items.significance: Expresses a Judean perspective welcoming Persian rule; compare the Cyrus Cylinder.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Jewish/Hebrew Bible
items.date: Texts composed c. 8th–2nd centuries BCE; surviving witnesses range from c. 600 BCE onward
details: Much composition took place during or after the exile; Ketef Hinnom amulets (~600 BCE) and Dead Sea Scrolls are early partial witnesses.
Complete Hebrew manuscripts are medieval; distinguish composition dates from surviving copies.
items.significance: The text is later and more layered than many events it describes. Check the “Price is Right” slides.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide
items.periodLabel: composition and manuscript history spans periods

items.name: Dead Sea Scrolls
details: About 900 manuscripts in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek; include biblical and sectarian texts.
They preserve the oldest copies of almost every biblical book.
items.significance: Show the diversity of Second Temple Judaism and provide the earliest biblical manuscript copies.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Alexander the Great
items.location: Macedonia; Achaemenid Empire and successor territories
details: Conquered the Achaemenid Empire, burned Persepolis, and died in Babylon.
His generals divided the empire, including Seleucus and the Seleucid dynasty.
items.significance: Marks the start of the Hellenistic period and the spread of Hellenism.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Seleucid statue of Herakles-Bahram
items.date: Hellenistic period; exact date/place to check with slides
details: Greek hero Herakles is identified with the Iranian victory god Verethragna (Bahram).
The statue bears a Greek inscription.
items.significance: Shows Hellenism as cultural blending rather than replacement. Check the slide for date and place.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Paul's Letter to the Galatians
items.location: Greek letter to churches in Galatia, central Anatolia (Roman Empire)
details: Paul argues that gentile converts do not need circumcision or Torah observance.
Galatians 3:28 states “neither Jew nor Greek.”
items.significance: Shows early Christianity defining its relationship with Judaism and addressing ethnic identity.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Account of the Deeds of Ardashir
items.date: Ardashir I’s reign, 224–242 CE; text in Middle Persian
details: Legend recounts Ardashir’s rise and overthrow of the Parthian king Artabanus.
Divine royal glory guides Ardashir.
items.significance: Legitimizes the new dynasty by joining kingship with Zoroastrian favor.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Investiture of Ardashir I at Naqsh-e Rostam
details: Ahura Mazda on horseback hands Ardashir the ring of kingship; horses trample Artabanus and Ahriman.
A trilingual inscription accompanies the relief, placed near Achaemenid royal tombs.
items.significance: Claims divine legitimacy and Persian heritage for Sasanian kingship.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Magic Bowls
details: Clay bowls carry spiral incantations in Jewish Aramaic, Syriac, or Mandaic.
They were buried upside down to trap demons; the practice crossed religious communities.
items.significance: Shows everyday religious diversity in the Sasanian Empire.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Orientalism
items.location: Western representations of the Middle East
details: Western discourse pictures “the East” as exotic, backward, and unchanging.
Such representations can justify domination and shape accounts of the ancient Middle East, such as despotic eastern kings versus free Greeks.
items.significance: Names a lens the course questions when studying the ancient Middle East.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Sedentary vs Mobile Populations
items.location: Mesopotamia and the wider Middle East
details: Settled farmers contrast with pastoralists and foragers; Scott discusses this in Against the Grain.
States relied on taxable grain farmers, while Mesopotamian texts stereotyped mobile peoples such as the Amorites.
items.significance: Ancient difference could be based on lifestyle rather than physical traits.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Race and Ethnicity
details: Ethnicity is a social grouping, internally or externally defined, often through cultural features such as food or language.
Race is also social and rests on essentialized difference that creates hierarchy; Mesopotamian distinctions emphasized lifestyle rather than physical or linguistic traits.
items.significance: Distinguishes ethnicity from race and cautions against projecting modern US racial categories unchanged onto antiquity.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Racial hinge/loophole
items.date: Early 20th-century naturalization cases to the present
items.location: United States; Middle Eastern and Iranian American experience
details: Racial loophole: Middle Eastern (especially Iranian) Americans can be legally classified as white while facing social discrimination.
Racial hinge: a court ruling about the whiteness of one group can shift how adjacent groups are classified; the lecture contrasts Armenian Christian and Persian Zoroastrian cases.
items.significance: Shows race as a social and legal construction. Check the author in notes.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Hellenism
items.location: Seleucid realms and wider eastern Mediterranean/western Asia
details: Greek language and culture spread and were adopted locally after Alexander.
Local traditions blended with Greek forms, as in Herakles-Bahram; “Greek” also became an identity label.
items.significance: Describes cultural mixing rather than replacement.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Judaism (ancient)
items.date: Exile and Persian period through Late Antiquity
items.location: Judea and Jewish communities across the diaspora
details: Religion of Judeans centered on YHWH, Torah, and the Jerusalem Temple.
Diverse Second Temple practices are evidenced by the Dead Sea Scrolls; after the Temple’s destruction in 70 CE, rabbinic Judaism and Babylonian Jewish communities developed.
items.significance: Shows a changing and diverse tradition across imperial settings.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Christianity (ancient)
items.date: 1st century CE onward; state-backed in Roman Empire from 4th century CE
items.location: Roman Judea, Roman/Byzantine Empire, and Sasanian Empire
details: Grew from the Jewish Jesus movement; Paul spread it to gentiles, as seen in Galatians.
Became state-backed in the Roman/Byzantine Empire from the 4th century CE and was also present in the Sasanian Empire.
items.significance: An example of a Late Antique state religion and a movement with Jewish origins.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: Zoroastrianism (ancient)
details: Iranian religion centered on Ahura Mazda and the opposition of the evil spirit Ahriman; traditions include fire temples and the Avesta.
Achaemenid kings invoked Ahuramazda; Sasanians made Zoroastrianism a state religion, as represented at Naqsh-e Rostam.
items.significance: Shows the relationship between kingship and religion in a diverse empire.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: T/F: Race is a biological category while ethnicity is cultural
details: False: race and ethnicity are both social categories.
Race rests on essentialized difference that establishes hierarchy.
items.significance: Corrects the myth of race as biological fact and supports careful analysis of group identity.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide

items.name: T/F: Hammurabi wrote the first law code ever
details: False: earlier law collections existed, including the laws of Ur-Namma.
Hammurabi’s stele is a royal monument and a class example of royal propaganda.
items.significance: Corrects the course myth that Hammurabi produced the earliest law code.
items.source: User card list; Test 1 Study Guide
